title: Cables Whose Loss Splits the Network
statement:
A data center has n servers numbered 0 to n − 1. cables[i] = [a, b] is a two-way cable between servers a and b. Right now every server can reach every other one, and no two cables join the same pair.

A cable is critical if cutting it alone leaves some pair of servers unable to reach each other. Return every critical cable as [a, b]. The list may be in any order, and each pair may list its two servers in either order.

examples.why: Servers 0, 1, 2 form a loop, so any one of those cables has a detour. Cable 2–3 is critical even though neither end is a dead end.
A ring: cutting any one cable leaves the long way round.
The only cable holds the network together.

constraints: The network is connected and has no repeated cables
hints: Brute force: cut each cable in turn and check if the network is still connected. That is O(E · (V + E)). What property of a cable makes it safe to cut?
A cable is safe exactly when it lies on a cycle. In a DFS tree, a cycle shows up as a back edge from a node to one of its ancestors.

Number nodes in DFS visit order (disc) and compute low[u], the smallest visit number reachable from u's subtree using one back edge. The tree edge parent→u is critical exactly when low[u] > disc[parent].

explain.intuition:
A cable can be cut safely if and only if it sits on some loop: the loop is the detour. So the task is to find tree edges that no loop passes over.

Run a DFS and stamp each server with its visit time disc. Every non-tree edge in an undirected DFS goes to an ancestor, which closes a loop. For each node u, compute low[u]: the earliest visit time that anything in u's subtree can reach with one such back edge. If low[u] is still later than the parent's time, nothing below u can climb back above the parent without the parent→u cable, so that cable is critical. This is Tarjan's bridge-finding algorithm, and it needs just one DFS.
steps: Build an adjacency list that stores (neighbour, cable id) pairs.
DFS from server 0. On first visit set disc[u] = low[u] = time++.
For each neighbour v reached by a cable other than the one you came in on: if unvisited, recurse, then set low[u] = min(low[u], low[v]); if visited, set low[u] = min(low[u], disc[v]).
After returning from child v, if low[v] > disc[u], record cable [u, v].
Use an explicit stack in practice: a chain of 100 000 servers overflows a recursive DFS.
pitfalls: Letting a node use the cable back to its own parent as a "back edge". Then low always reaches the parent and no cable is ever critical. Skip the incoming cable by id.
Using ≥ instead of >. low[v] == disc[u] means a loop returns to u, so cable u–v is on that loop and is safe. (≥ is the test for critical servers, not cables.)
Assuming only cables to dead-end servers are critical. Cable 2–3 in the first example joins two busy parts.

solutions.title: Cut each cable and test connectivity
solutions.idea: For every cable, search from one end without using it. If the other end is unreachable, the cable is critical.

solutions.title: Tarjan's bridges with an explicit stack
solutions.idea: One DFS computes visit times and low-links. A tree cable parent→u is critical when low[u] > disc[parent].

followups: Find the critical servers instead: those whose failure disconnects the network. What changes in the low-link test?
Two cables may now join the same pair of servers. Why does skipping the parent by cable id, not by node, matter now?
